newsitem.title: JORDAN: World Bank to offer Jordan $1 bln assistance.
newsitem.headline: World Bank to offer Jordan $1 bln assistance.

text.p: The World Bank could extend to Jordan around $1 billion during a new five-year economic reform phase to start next year, a bank official said on Sunday.

"We have said to the government that we are ready to support the continuation of the reform programme within the framework of the next five-year plan," Kemal Dervis, World Bank vice president for the Middle East and North Africa, told reporters.

He said it was too early to give details before the new government outlines Jordan's next structural adjustment programme, but a World Bank official said most of the assistance would be in the form of loans.
Jordan is formulating a five-year reform plan to start after a three-year IMF reform programme, which saw some progress towards liberalising the economy, ends this year.

The 1995-1997 reform programme follows a successful monetary and fiscal stabilisation programme under IMF guidance that Jordan went through since an economic crisis in 1989 that wiped out its reserves.

Dervis, who met senior Jordanian officials during a regional tour, said the World Bank "could have for Jordan a substantial amount of financial backing" to the tune of $1 billion for the government's coming five-year reform phase.
"I can give a very rough figure of $1 billion that could be available from the World Bank for the next five-year period," Dervis said.
Dervis said that the World Bank. which "was committed to continuing support for the overall reform process", would allocate a substantial part of its aid to sectoral projects.
But the assistance in transport, power, health, education and water schemes still needed to be formulated with the government to set both priorities and allocations.

Dervis said the World Bank agreed with the government's assessment that an annual growth rate of between sex and seven percent was needed to ensure that reforms filter to ordinary Jordanians by the end of the decade. Jordan has had an average five percent growth in the last few years.

Many businessmen and economists privately criticise the government for the slow pace of reform, especially towards privatisation, which successive governments have committed themselves to but which has so far been piecemeal.
"Now that Jordan has stabilised, you have put the house in order, now is the time to generate results for the people," he added.
